 November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Joe Ashwell
 First reported on New Civil Engineer 
 30 Second Briefing
 Entries have opened for New Civil Engineer’s inaugural Floods & Water Awards, featuring 21 categories spanning project delivery, technical innovation and long-term community impact in flood and water management. Categories cover areas such as flood risk schemes, drainage and SuDS, asset resilience, digital tools and data-led decision-making, and organisational or individual contributions. The programme gives geotechnical, civil and water engineers a platform to benchmark approaches to flood defence design, catchment-scale planning and resilience upgrades against UK best practice.
 Technical Brief
 Awards framework explicitly separates “projects, innovation and impact” from “organisation and contribution”, encouraging distinct safety lenses.
 Category structure enables direct comparison of emergency-response planning, operational flood safety and long-term residual-risk management.
 Entry portal groups categories behind a single online interface, standardising submitted safety evidence and documentation formats.
 Digital submission route encourages inclusion of monitoring data, hydraulic models and geotechnical design outputs as safety proof.
 Cross-cutting focus on both floods and wider water management promotes integration of SuDS, drainage and defence operations into one risk regime.
 Recognition of organisational and individual contributions incentivises formalisation of safety leadership, training and incident-learning processes.
 For similar schemes, such award taxonomies often become de facto benchmarks when auditing flood and water safety practice.
 Our Take
 With 21 categories, the Floods & Water Awards sit at the more granular end of NCE’s awards portfolio, which in our database also includes broader schemes like the British Construction & Infrastructure Awards and NCE Bridges Awards that tend to focus on multi-hazard infrastructure performance rather than a single risk type.
 NCE’s recent early-careers initiatives and challenges (such as the Bridges Conference competitions and the Heathrow innovation competition) suggest that the Floods & Water Awards could be a useful route for younger practitioners and smaller consultancies to gain visibility for novel flood-risk and water-management approaches that might not yet be deployed at major project scale.

 Related Articles
 Hazards 8 days ago South London partial building collapse: stability lessons for urban engineers
 Residents of 14 properties evacuated after the partial collapse of three terraced houses in south London have been allowed back home more than 11 weeks after the incident. Structural engineers have evidently deemed the remaining buildings stable enough for reoccupation following inspections and temporary works to secure the damaged terrace. The case underlines the time and access constraints that follow even localised collapse events, with extended exclusion zones needed while assessing party wall integrity, shared foundations and potential progressive failure in dense urban streets.
 Hazards 9 days ago Habas Demir Celik blast in Turkey: crane and furnace safety lessons for engineers
 A blast at the Habas Demir Celik iron and steel plant in Aliaga, Izmir province, killed 16 workers when a ceiling crane snapped and fell into an arc furnace during molten steel casting around noon on 9 November. Ten people remain trapped under rubble, while 13 were injured and two are in serious condition, with casualties distributed across several regional hospitals. The Turkish government has opened an investigation, putting overhead crane integrity, furnace-area lifting operations and maintenance regimes under immediate scrutiny for heavy steel plants.
 Hazards 13 days ago Codelco Andina tailings spill: incident and water-risk lessons for engineers
 Codelco has halted processing at its Andina copper division after an obstruction in the tailings transport system near the Rápido RV4 sector caused a partial tailings release that may have entered the Blanco River within the Río Blanco canyon, upstream of the Aconcagua River basin. Emergency actions include shutting the concentrator, suspending tailings transport, diverting flows to the Piuquenitos reservoir, and continuous river sampling, while water utility Esval has closed its Aconcagua surface intake and switched to underground sources for Los Andes. The incident coincides with disclosure of 42,100 tonnes of previously inflated copper output and a 17,000‑tonne inventory reporting discrepancy, intensifying regulatory and community scrutiny of tailings and water-risk management at Andina.
